Global well-posedness issues for the inviscid Boussinesq system with Yudovich’s type dataThanks: 1Université Paris-Est, Laboratoire d’Analyse et de Mathématiques Appliquées, UMR 8050, 61 avenue du Général de Gaulle, 94010 Créteil Cedex, France. E-mail: danchin@@univ-paris12.frThanks: 2Université Paris 11, Laboratoire de Mathématiques, Bâtiment 425, 91405 Orsay Cedex, France. E-mail: marius.paicu@@math.u-psud.fr

Raphaël Danchin1 and Marius Paicu2
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

The present paper is dedicated to the study of the global existence for the inviscid two-dimensional Boussinesq system. We focus on finite energy data with bounded vorticity and we find out that, under quite a natural additional assumption on the initial temperature, there exists a global unique solution. None smallness conditions are imposed on the data. The global existence issues for infinite energy initial velocity, and for the Bénard system are also discussed.

Introduction

The incompressible Euler equations have been intensively studied from a mathematical viewpoint. The present paper aims at extending the celebrated result by Yudovich concerning the two-dimensional Euler system (see [17]) to the following two-dimensional Boussinesq system:

(Bκ,ν) {∂tθ+u⋅∇θ−κ​Δ​θ=0∂tu+u⋅∇u−ν​Δ​u+∇Π=θ​e2withe2=(0,1),div​u=0.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}\theta+u\cdot\nabla\theta-\kappa\Delta\theta=0\\ \partial_{t}u+u\cdot\nabla u-\nu\Delta u+\nabla\Pi=\theta\,e_{2}\quad\hbox{with}\quad e_{2}=(0,1),\\ \,\mbox{\rm div}\,u=0.\end{cases}

The above system describes the evolution of the velocity field uu of a two-dimensional incompressible fluid moving under a vertical force the magnitude θ\theta of which is transported with or without diffusion by u.u. Above the molecular diffusion parameter κ\kappa and viscosity ν\nu are nonnegative, and Π\Pi stands for the pressure in the fluid. For the sake of simplicity, we restrict our attention to the case where the space variable xx belongs to the whole plan ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} (our results extend with no difficulty to periodic boundary conditions, though).

The Boussinesq system is of relevance to study a number of models coming from atmospheric or oceanographic turbulence where rotation and stratification play an important role (see e.g. [15]). The scalar function θ\theta may for instance represent temperature variation in a gravity field, and θ​e2,\theta\,e_{2}, the buoyancy force.

From the mathematical point of view, if both κ\kappa and ν\nu are positive then standard energy methods yield global existence of smooth solutions for arbitrarily large data (see e.g. [5, 12]). In contrast, in the case when κ=ν=0,\kappa=\nu=0, the Boussinesq system exhibits vorticity intensification and the global well-posedness issue remains an unsolved challenging open problem (except if θ0\theta_{0} is a constant of course) which may be formally compared to the similar problem for the three-dimensional axisymmetric Euler equations with swirl (see e.g. [10] for more explanations).

As pointed out by H. K. Moffatt in [14], knowing whether having κ>0\kappa>0 or ν>0\nu>0 precludes the formation of finite time singularities is an important issue. In [9], we stated that in the case κ=0\kappa=0 and ν>0\nu>0 no such formation may be encountered for finite energy initial data. More precisely, we stated that for any (θ0,u0)(\theta_{0},u_{0}) in L2​(ℝ2)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) with div​u0=0,\,\mbox{\rm div}\,u_{0}=0, System (B0,ν)(B_{0,\nu}) has a unique global finite energy solution.

In the present paper, we aim at investigating the opposite case, namely κ>0\kappa>0 and ν=0.\nu=0. The corresponding Boussinesq system thus reads

(Bκ,0) {∂tθ+u⋅∇θ−κ​Δ​θ=0∂tu+u⋅∇u+∇Π=θ​e2div​u=0\begin{cases}\partial_{t}\theta+u\cdot\nabla\theta-\kappa\Delta\theta=0\\ \partial_{t}u+u\cdot\nabla u+\nabla\Pi=\theta\,e_{2}\\ \,\mbox{\rm div}\,u=0\end{cases}

and may be seen as a coupling between the two-dimensional Euler equations and a transport-diffusion equation. In passing, let us point out that in the case θ≡0,\theta\equiv 0, System (Bκ,0)(B_{\kappa,0}) reduces to the Euler equation.

It is well known that the standard Euler equation is globally well-posed in HsH^{s} for any s>2.s>2. A similar result has been stated for (Bκ,0)(B_{\kappa,0}) in the case s≥3s\geq 3 by D. Chae in [6], then extended to rough data by T. Hmidi and S. Keraani in [13]. There, global well-posedness is shown whenever the initial velocity u0u_{0} belongs to Bp,11+2pB^{1+\frac{2}{p}}_{p,1} and the initial temperature θ0\theta_{0} is in LrL^{r} for some (p,r)(p,r) satisfying 2<r≤p≤∞2<r\leq p\leq\infty (plus a technical condition if p=r=∞p=r=\infty). Let us emphasize that in the Besov spaces framework, the assumption on u0u_{0} is somewhat optimal (since it is optimal for the standard Euler equations, see [16]).

Here we want to state global existence for less regular data satisfying Yudovich’s type conditions. Roughly, we want to consider data (θ0,u0)(\theta_{0},u_{0}) in L2L^{2} such that the initial vorticity ω0:=∂1v02−∂2v01\omega_{0}:=\partial_{1}v_{0}^{2}-\partial_{2}v_{0}^{1} is bounded. Note however that, since we expect the corresponding solution to have bounded vorticity for all positive time, we have to introduce an additional assumption on θ0.\theta_{0}. Indeed, the vorticity equation reads

∂tω+u⋅∇ω=∂1θ.\partial_{t}\omega+u\cdot\nabla\omega=\partial_{1}\theta.

Therefore, since no gain of smoothness may be expected from the above transport equation, having ω\omega bounded requires that ∂1θ∈Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,L∞).\partial_{1}\theta\in L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{\infty}). Now, considering that θ\theta satisfies the following heat equation

∂tθ−κΔθ=fwithf:=−u⋅∇θ,\partial_{t}\theta-\kappa\Delta\theta=f\quad\hbox{with}\quad f:=-u\cdot\nabla\theta,

the assumptions on θ0\theta_{0} should ensure that

(1) ∇eκ​t​Δθ0∈Ll​o​c1(ℝ+;L∞)\nabla e^{\kappa t\Delta}\theta_{0}\in L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{\infty})

where (eλ​Δ)λ>0(e^{\lambda\Delta})_{\lambda>0} stands for the heat semi-group.

It turns out that (1) is equivalent to having ∇θ0\nabla\theta_{0} in the nonhomogeneous Besov space B∞,1−2B^{-2}_{\infty,1} (see e.g. [3]). This motivates the following statement which is the main result of the paper:

Theorem 1.

Let θ0∈L2∩B∞,1−1\theta_{0}\in L^{2}\cap B^{-1}_{\infty,1} and u0∈L2u_{0}\in L^{2} with div​u0=0.\,\mbox{\rm div}\,u_{0}=0. Assume in addition that the initial vorticity ω0\omega_{0} belongs to Lr∩L∞L^{r}\cap L^{\infty} for some r≥2.r\geq 2. System (Bκ,0)(B_{\kappa,0}) admits a unique global solution (θ,u)(\theta,u) satisfying

(2) θ∈𝒞⁡(ℝ+,L2∩B∞,1−1)∩Ll​o​c2​(ℝ+,H1)∩Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,B∞,11),u∈𝒞0,1l​o​c(ℝ+;L2) and ω∈L∞l​o​c(ℝ+;Lr∩L∞).\begin{array}[]{c}\theta\in{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2}\cap B^{-1}_{\infty,1})\cap L^{2}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{1})\cap L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};B^{1}_{\infty,1}),\\[6.45831pt] u\in{\mathcal{C}}^{0,1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2})\ \hbox{ and }\ \omega\in L^{\infty}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{r}\cap L^{\infty}).\end{array}
Remark 1.

As a by-product of our proof, we gather that if in addition θ0∈Lp\theta_{0}\in L^{p} (resp. u0∈B∞,11u_{0}\in B^{1}_{\infty,1}) for some p∈[1,+∞]p\in[1,+\infty] then θ∈L∞​(ℝ+,Lp)\theta\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{p}) (resp. u∈𝒞⁡(ℝ+,B∞,11)u\in{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};B^{1}_{\infty,1})).

Remark 2.

The B∞,1−1B^{-1}_{\infty,1} hypothesis over θ0\theta_{0} is quite mild compared to the L2L^{2} hypothesis. Indeed, it may be shown that L2L^{2} is continuously embedded in the Besov space B∞,2−1B^{-1}_{\infty,2} which is slightly larger than B∞,1−1.B^{-1}_{\infty,1}.

The paper unfolds as follows. In the first section, we prove Theorem 1. In the second section, motivated by the fact that having u0u_{0} in L2L^{2} and ω0∈L1\omega_{0}\in L^{1} requires the vorticity to have zero average over ℝ2,\mathbb{R}^{2}, we consider initial velocities which are L2L^{2} perturbations of infinite energy smooth stationary solutions for the incompressible Euler equations. Some extensions to Theorem 1 are discussed in the third section. A few technical inequalities have been postponed in the appendix.

1. Proof of Theorem 1

Proving Theorem 1 requires our using the (nonhomogeneous) Littlewood-Paley decomposition. One can proceed as in [7]: first we consider a dyadic partition of unity:

1=χ⁡(ξ)+∑q≥0φ⁡(2−q​ξ),1=\chi(\xi)+\sum\limits_{q\geq 0}\varphi(2^{-q}\xi),

for some nonnegative function χ∈𝒞∞​(B⁡(0,43))\chi\in{\mathcal{C}}^{\infty}(B(0,\frac{4}{3})) with value 11 over the ball B⁡(0,34),B(0,\frac{3}{4}), and φ⁡(ξ):=χ⁡(ξ/2)−χ⁡(ξ)\varphi(\xi):=\chi(\xi/2)-\chi(\xi).

Next, we introduce the dyadic blocks Δq\Delta_{q} of our decomposition by setting

Δqu:=0 if q≤−2,Δ−1u:=ℱ−1(χℱu)andΔqu:=ℱ−1(φ(2−q⋅)ℱu) if q≥0.\Delta_{q}u:=0\ \hbox{ if }\ q\leq-2,\qquad\Delta_{-1}u:={\mathcal{F}}^{-1}(\chi{\mathcal{F}}u)\quad\hbox{and}\quad\Delta_{q}u:={\mathcal{F}}^{-1}(\varphi(2^{-q}\cdot){\mathcal{F}}u)\ \text{ if }\ q\geq 0.

One may prove that for all tempered distribution uu the following Littlewood-Paley decomposition holds true:

u=∑q≥−1Δq​u.u=\sum\limits_{q\geq-1}\Delta_{q}u.

For s∈ℝ,s\in\mathbb{R}, p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty] and r∈[1,∞],r\in[1,\infty], one can now define the nonhomogeneous Besov space Bp,rs:=Bp,rs​(ℝ2)B^{s}_{p,r}:=B^{s}_{p,r}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) as the set of tempered distributions uu over ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} so that

‖u‖Bp,rs​(ℝ2):=‖2q​s​‖Δq​u‖Lp​(ℝ2)‖ℓr​(ℤ)<∞.\|u\|_{B^{s}_{p,r}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}:=\bigl\|2^{qs}\|\Delta_{q}u\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\bigr\|_{\ell^{r}(\mathbb{Z})}<\infty.

We shall also use several times the following well-known fact for incompressible fluid mechanics (see the proof in e.g. [7], Chap. 3):

Proposition 1.

For any p∈]1,∞[p\in]1,\infty[ the operator ω↦∇u\omega\mapsto\nabla u is bounded in Lp.L^{p}. More precisely, there exists a constant CC such that

‖∇u‖Lp≤C​p2p−1​‖ω‖Lp.\|\nabla u\|_{L^{p}}\leq C\frac{p^{2}}{p-1}\,\|\omega\|_{L^{p}}.

One can now tackle the proof of Theorem 1. One shall proceed as follows.

  1. 1.

    We smooth out the data so as to get a sequence of global smooth solutions to (Bκ,0).(B_{\kappa,0}).

  2. 2.

    Energy estimates are proved.

  3. 3.

    We establish estimates in larger norms.

  4. 4.

    We state uniform estimates for the first order time derivatives.

  5. 5.

    We pass to the limit in the system by means of compactness arguments.

  6. 6.

    Uniqueness is proved.

First step.

We smooth out the initial data (θ0,u0)(\theta_{0},u_{0}) (use e.g. a convolution process) and get a sequence of smooth initial data (θ0n,u0n)n∈ℕ(\theta_{0}^{n},u_{0}^{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} which is bounded in the space given in the statement of the theorem. In addition, those smooth data belong to all the Sobolev spaces Hs.H^{s}. Hence, applying Chae’s result [6] provides us with a sequence of smooth global solutions (θn,un)n∈ℕ(\theta^{n},u^{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} which belong to all the spaces 𝒞⁡(ℝ+,Hs).{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{s}). From system (Bκ,0)(B_{\kappa,0}) and standard product laws in Sobolev spaces, we deduce that (θn,un)(\theta^{n},u^{n}) belongs to 𝒞1​(ℝ+,Hs){\mathcal{C}}^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{s}) for all s∈ℝ,s\in\mathbb{R}, and thus also to 𝒞1​(ℝ+,Lp){\mathcal{C}}^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{p}) for all p∈[2,∞].p\in[2,\infty]. This will be more than enough to make the computations in the following two steps rigorous.

According to the previous steps, we have

2. A global result for infinite energy initial velocity

In dimension two, the assumption that u0u_{0} is in L2L^{2} is somewhat restrictive since it entails that the vorticity ω0\omega_{0} has 00 average over ℝ2.\mathbb{R}^{2}. This in particular precludes our considering vortex patches like structures or, more generally, data with compactly supported nonnegative vorticity. The present section aims at generalizing our study to initial velocity fields with (possibly) infinite energy. The functional setting we shall introduce below is borrowed from Chemin’s in [7].

Let us first notice that whenever gg is a radial 𝒞c∞{\mathcal{C}}_{c}^{\infty} function supported away from the origin then the smooth vector field σ\sigma defined by

(22) σ⁡(x)=x⊥|x|2​∫0|x|r​g​(r)​𝑑r\sigma(x)=\frac{x^{\bot}}{|x|^{2}}\int_{0}^{|x|}rg(r)\,dr

is a stationary solution to the two-dimensional incompressible Euler equations, and has vorticity ωσ:x↦g⁡(|x|).\omega_{\sigma}:x\mapsto g(|x|).

For m∈ℝ,m\in\mathbb{R}, we then define EmE_{m} as the set of all divergence-free L2L^{2} perturbations of a velocity field σ\sigma satisfying (22) and

(23) ∫ℝ2g⁡(|x|)​𝑑x=m.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}g(|x|)\,dx=m.

Showing that the definition of EmE_{m} depends only on mm is left to the reader (it is only a matter of using Fourier variables).

The rest of this section is devoted to the proof of the following generalization of Theorem 1.

Theorem 2.

Let θ0∈L2∩B∞,1−1\theta_{0}\in L^{2}\cap B^{-1}_{\infty,1} and u0∈Emu_{0}\in E_{m} for some m∈ℝ.m\in\mathbb{R}. Assume in addition that the initial vorticity ω0\omega_{0} belongs to Lr∩L∞L^{r}\cap L^{\infty} for some r≥2.r\geq 2. Then System (Bκ,0)(B_{\kappa,0}) admits a unique global solution (θ,u)(\theta,u) such that

(24) θ∈𝒞⁡(ℝ+,L2∩B∞,11)∩Ll​o​c2​(ℝ+,H1)∩Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,B∞,11),u∈𝒞l​o​c0,1​(ℝ+,Em)​ and ​ω∈Ll​o​c∞​(ℝ+,Lr∩L∞).\begin{array}[]{c}\theta\in{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2}\cap B^{1}_{\infty,1})\cap L^{2}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{1})\cap L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};B^{1}_{\infty,1}),\\[6.45831pt] u\in{\mathcal{C}}^{0,1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};E_{m})\ \hbox{ and }\ \omega\in L^{\infty}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{r}\cap L^{\infty}).\end{array}

Proof:  As it is very similar to that of Theorem 1, we just sketch the proof and point out what has to be changed.

Throughout we fix a stationary vector-field σ\sigma satisfying (22) and (23). Setting u=v+σ,u=v+\sigma, System (Bκ,0)(B_{\kappa,0}) rewrites

(25) {∂tθ+(v+σ)⋅∇θ−κ​Δ​θ=0∂tv+(v+σ)⋅∇v+v⋅∇σ+∇Π=θ​e2div​v=0.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}\theta+(v+\sigma)\cdot\nabla\theta-\kappa\Delta\theta=0\\ \partial_{t}v+(v+\sigma)\cdot\nabla v+v\cdot\nabla\sigma+\nabla\Pi=\theta\,e_{2}\\ \,\mbox{\rm div}\,v=0.\end{cases}

As div​σ=div​v=0,\,\mbox{\rm div}\,\sigma=\,\mbox{\rm div}\,v=0, the energy estimates for θ\theta remain the same. As for the velocity field, having the new term v⋅∇σv\cdot\nabla\sigma in the equation implies that

and using Bernstein inequality, we readily get

In order to prove the uniqueness, it is fundamental to notice that if (θ1,u1)(\theta_{1},u_{1}) and (θ2,u2)(\theta_{2},u_{2}) both solve (Bκ,0)(B_{\kappa,0}) with the same data, and satisfy (24) with the same mm (an assumption which is not restrictive since we know that u1u_{1} and u2u_{2} coincide initially) then one may write u1=σ+v1u_{1}=\sigma+v_{1} and u2=σ+v2u_{2}=\sigma+v_{2} for some stationary vector-field σ\sigma satisfying (22),(23) and v1,v2v_{1},v_{2} in Ll​o​c∞​(ℝ+,L2).L^{\infty}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2}).

{∂tδθ+u2⋅∇δθ−κΔδθ=−δv⋅∇θ1,∂tδv+u2⋅∇δv+∇δΠ=−δv⋅∇u1+δθe2−δv⋅∇σ.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\delta\!\theta+u_{2}\cdot\nabla\delta\!\theta-\kappa\Delta\delta\!\theta=-\delta\!v\cdot\nabla\theta_{1},\\[4.30554pt] \partial_{t}\delta\!v+u_{2}\cdot\nabla\delta\!v+\nabla\delta\!\Pi=-\delta\!v\cdot\nabla u_{1}+\delta\!\theta\,e_{2}-\delta\!v\cdot\nabla\sigma.\end{array}\right.

‖δ​v⋅∇σ‖L2≤‖δ​v‖L2​‖∇σ‖L∞,\|\delta\!v\cdot\nabla\sigma\|_{L^{2}}\leq\|\delta\!v\|_{L^{2}}\|\nabla\sigma\|_{L^{\infty}},

the energy bounds for the above system are the same as in the case σ=0.\sigma=0. Hence, from argument similar to those used in the previous section, it is easy to conclude the proof of uniqueness. The details are left to the reader.  

3. Further results and concluding remarks

In this concluding section, we list a few extensions which may be obtained by straightforward generalizations of our method.

3.1. Remarks concerning the Boussinesq system

Let us stress that the key to the proof of Theorems 1 and 2 is that, on the one hand, the solution does not develop singularities as long as

∫0T‖∇θ‖L∞​𝑑t<∞,\int_{0}^{T}\|\nabla\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}\,dt<\infty,

and that, on the other hand, under quite weak assumptions over the initial data, the above integral remains finite for all T<∞.T<\infty.

In fact, a quick revisitation of our proof shows that if one assumes in addition that ω0∈Cε\omega_{0}\in C^{\varepsilon} and θ0∈C−1+ε\theta_{0}\in C^{-1+\varepsilon} (with C−1+ε:=B∞,∞−1+εC^{-1+\varepsilon}:=B^{-1+\varepsilon}_{\infty,\infty}) for some ε∈]0,1[\varepsilon\in]0,1[ then both ∇θ\nabla\theta and ∇u\nabla u are in Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,L∞​(ℝ2))L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})) so that the additional Hölder regularity is conserved during the evolution. We believe that, more generally, our study opens a way to investigate vortex patches structures (or striated regularity) for the Boussinesq system with κ>0\kappa>0 and ν=0.\nu=0.

Let us also emphasize that if, in addition to the hypotheses of Theorem 1, we have u0∈B∞,11u_{0}\in B^{1}_{\infty,1} then the corresponding solution (θ,u)(\theta,u) also satisfies

u∈𝒞⁡(ℝ+,B∞,11).u\in{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};B^{1}_{\infty,1}).

Indeed, according to a result by M. Vishik in [16] concerning the transport equation, one can propagate the B∞,10B^{0}_{\infty,1} regularity over the vorticity ω\omega provided ∂1θ\partial_{1}\theta is in Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,B∞,10)L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};B^{0}_{\infty,1}) and there exists some universal constant CC such that

(27) ‖ω⁡(t)‖B∞,10≤C⁡(1+∫0t‖∇u‖L∞)​(‖ω0‖B∞,10+∫0t‖∂1θ‖B∞,10).\|\omega(t)\|_{B^{0}_{\infty,1}}\leq C\biggl(1+\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla u\|_{L^{\infty}}\biggr)\biggl(\|\omega_{0}\|_{B^{0}_{\infty,1}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\partial_{1}\theta\|_{B^{0}_{\infty,1}}\biggr).

Now, under the sole assumptions of Theorem 1, one may bound ∂1θ\partial_{1}\theta in Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,B∞,10)L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};B^{0}_{\infty,1}) by means of the norms of the data. Because, owing to B∞,10↪L∞B^{0}_{\infty,1}\hookrightarrow L^{\infty} and (14), one may write

‖∇u‖L∞≤C⁡(‖u‖L2+‖ω‖B∞,10),\|\nabla u\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C\bigl(\|u\|_{L^{2}}+\|\omega\|_{B^{0}_{\infty,1}}\bigr),

Inequality (27) combined with Gronwall lemma ensures the conservation of the additional B∞,10B^{0}_{\infty,1} regularity for the vorticity (and thus of the B∞,11B^{1}_{\infty,1} regularity for the velocity). This argument provides another proof of Hmidi and Keraani’s result in [13] under somewhat weaker assumptions over θ0\theta_{0} (there having θ0\theta_{0} in (a subspace of) L∞L^{\infty} was needed).

3.2. The Bénard system

Our method may also be adapted with almost no change to the study of the following Bénard system:

(28) {∂tθ+u⋅∇θ−κ​Δ​θ=u2∂tu+u⋅∇u+∇p=θ​e2(θ,u)|t=0=(θ0,u0),\begin{cases}\partial_{t}\theta+u\cdot\nabla\theta-\kappa\Delta\theta=u_{2}\\ \partial_{t}u+u\cdot\nabla u+\nabla p=\theta\,e_{2}\\ (\theta,u)|_{t=0}=(\theta_{0},u_{0}),\end{cases}

which describes convective motions in a heated two-dimensional inviscid incompressible fluid under thermal effects (see e.g. [1], Chap. 6). We get

Theorem 3.

For all data (θ0,u0)(\theta_{0},u_{0}) with θ0∈L2∩B∞,1−1\theta_{0}\in L^{2}\cap B^{-1}_{\infty,1} and u0∈L2u_{0}\in L^{2} satisfying div​u0=0\,\mbox{\rm div}\,u_{0}=0 and ω0∈Lr∩L∞\omega_{0}\in L^{r}\cap L^{\infty} for some r∈[2,∞[,r\in[2,\infty[, System (28) has a unique global solution (θ,u)(\theta,u) such that

(29) θ∈𝒞⁡(ℝ+,L2∩B∞,11)∩Ll​o​c2​(ℝ+,H1)∩Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,B∞,11),u∈𝒞l​o​c0,1​(ℝ+,L2)​ and ​ω∈Ll​o​c∞​(ℝ+,Lr∩L∞).\begin{array}[]{c}\theta\in{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2}\cap B^{1}_{\infty,1})\cap L^{2}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{1})\cap L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};B^{1}_{\infty,1}),\\[6.45831pt] \quad u\in{\mathcal{C}}^{0,1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2})\ \hbox{ and }\ \omega\in L^{\infty}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{r}\cap L^{\infty}).\end{array}

Proof:  We just briefly indicate what has to be changed compared to the proof of Theorem 1. Owing to the new term u2u_{2} in the equation for the temperature, the energy estimates read

(30) 12​dd​t​‖θ‖L22+κ​‖∇θ‖L22=∫θ​u2​𝑑x,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|\theta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\kappa\|\nabla\theta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=\int\theta\>u_{2}\,dx,
(31) 12​dd​t​‖u‖L22=∫θ​u2​𝑑x.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|u\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=\int\theta\>u_{2}\,dx.

Adding up inequalities (30) and (31) yields

12​dd​t​‖(θ,u)​(t)‖L22+κ​‖∇θ‖L22=2​∫θ​u2​𝑑x,≤‖(θ,u)‖L22.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|(\theta,u)(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\kappa\|\nabla\theta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=2\displaystyle\int\theta\>u_{2}\,dx,\\ \leq\|(\theta,u)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}.

Thanks to the Gronwall inequality, we thus infer that

‖(θ,u)​(t)‖L22+2​κ​∫0t‖∇θ​(τ)‖L22​𝑑τ≤‖(θ0,u0)‖L22​e2​t.\|(\theta,u)(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+2\kappa\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla\theta(\tau)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\,d\tau\leq\|(\theta_{0},u_{0})\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\>e^{2t}.

The rest of the proof of Theorem 3 follows the lines of that of Theorem 1, once it has been noticed that the computations leading to Inequality (7) (see the appendix) also yield

‖∫0te(t−s)​κ​Δ​u2​(s)​𝑑s‖LT1​(B∞,11)≤C​∫0T‖u‖L∞​𝑑t.\bigg\|\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-s)\kappa\Delta}u_{2}(s)ds\bigg\|_{L_{T}^{1}(B^{1}_{\infty,1})}\leq C\int_{0}^{T}\|u\|_{L^{\infty}}\,dt.

Note also that having the new (lower order) term u2u_{2} in Equation (28)1\eqref{eq:benard}_{1} is harmless for proving uniqueness.  

Appendix

Here we prove a few inequalities which have been used throughout the paper.

Proof of Inequality (7): Assume that θ\theta satisfies

∂tθ−κΔθ=f,θ|t=0=θ0.\partial_{t}\theta-\kappa\Delta\theta=f,\qquad\theta_{|t=0}=\theta_{0}.

Then applying the dyadic operator Δq\Delta_{q} to the above equality yields

∂tΔq​θ−κ​Δq​Δ​θ=Δq​ffor all ​q≥−1.\partial_{t}\Delta_{q}\theta-\kappa\Delta_{q}\Delta\theta=\Delta_{q}f\quad\hbox{for all }\ q\geq-1.

From the maximum principle, we readily get

‖Δ−1​θ​(t)‖L∞≤‖Δ−1​θ0‖L∞+∫0t‖Δ−1​f​(τ)‖L∞​𝑑τ\|\Delta_{-1}\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|\Delta_{-1}\theta_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\Delta_{-1}f(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}\,d\tau

whence for all α∈[1,∞]\alpha\in[1,\infty] and t>0,t>0,

(32) ‖Δq​θ‖Lα​([0,t],L∞)≤C​t1α​(‖Δ−1​θ0‖L∞+‖Δ−1​f‖L1​([0,t],L∞)).\|\Delta_{q}\theta\|_{L^{\alpha}([0,t];L^{\infty})}\leq Ct^{\frac{1}{\alpha}}\Bigl(\|\Delta_{-1}\theta_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\Delta_{-1}f\|_{L^{1}([0,t];L^{\infty})}\Bigr).

Next, for bounding the high frequency blocks Δq​θ\Delta_{q}\theta with q≥0,q\geq 0, one may write

(33) Δq​θ​(t)=eκ​t​Δ​Δq​θ0+∫0teκ⁡(t−τ)​Δ​Δq​f​(τ)​𝑑τ\Delta_{q}\theta(t)=e^{\kappa t\Delta}\Delta_{q}\theta_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}e^{\kappa(t-\tau)\Delta}\Delta_{q}f(\tau)\,d\tau

where (eλ​Δ)λ>0(e^{\lambda\Delta})_{\lambda>0} stands for the heat semi-group, and take advantage of the following inequality stated by J.-Y. Chemin in [8]: there exists two positive constants cc and CC such that

(34) ‖eλ​Δ​Δq​g‖L∞≤C​e−c​λ​22​q​‖Δq​g‖L∞​ for all ​λ>0​ and ​q≥0.\|e^{\lambda\Delta}\Delta_{q}g\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq Ce^{-c\lambda 2^{2q}}\|\Delta_{q}g\|_{L^{\infty}}\ \hbox{ for all }\ \lambda>0\ \hbox{ and }\ q\geq 0.

From (33) and (34), we get

‖Δq​θ​(t)‖L∞≤C⁡(e−c​κ​22​q​t​‖Δq​θ0‖L∞+∫0te−c​κ​22​q​(t−τ)​‖Δq​f​(τ)‖L∞​𝑑τ).\|\Delta_{q}\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C\biggl(e^{-c\kappa 2^{2q}t}\|\Delta_{q}\theta_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}+\int_{0}^{t}e^{-c\kappa 2^{2q}(t-\tau)}\|\Delta_{q}f(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}\,d\tau\biggr).

Therefore, for all α∈[1,∞],\alpha\in[1,\infty], q≥0q\geq 0 and t>0,t>0,

κ1α​2(2α−1)​q​‖Δq​θ‖Lα​([0,t],L∞)≤C​2−q​(‖Δq​θ0‖L∞+‖Δq​f‖L1​([0,t],L∞)).\kappa^{\frac{1}{\alpha}}2^{(\frac{2}{\alpha}-1)q}\|\Delta_{q}\theta\|_{L^{\alpha}([0,t];L^{\infty})}\leq C2^{-q}\Bigl(\|\Delta_{q}\theta_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\Delta_{q}f\|_{L^{1}([0,t];L^{\infty})}\Bigr).

Summing on q≥0q\geq 0 and using (32), it is now easy to complete the proof of Inequality (7).  

Proof of Inequalities (14) and (15): For proving the first inequality, let us consider a L2L^{2} divergence free vector-field uu with bounded vorticity ω.\omega. As uu is in L2,L^{2}, one may write

u=∑q∈ℤΔ˙q​uwithΔ˙q:=φ⁡(2−q​D).u=\sum_{q\in\mathbb{Z}}\dot{\Delta}_{q}u\quad\hbox{with}\quad\dot{\Delta}_{q}:=\varphi(2^{-q}D).

Let NN be an integer parameter to be chosen hereafter. Given that u=−∇⟂(−Δ)−1​ωu=-\nabla^{\perp}(-\Delta)^{-1}\omega and using the Bernstein inequalities, we have

‖u‖L∞≤∑q≤N‖Δ˙q​u‖L∞+∑q>N‖Δ˙q​u‖L∞≤C​2N​‖u‖L2+C​∑q>N2−q​‖Δ˙q​ω‖L∞.\|u\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\sum\limits_{q\leq N}\|\dot{\Delta}_{q}u\|_{L^{\infty}}+\sum\limits_{q>N}\|\dot{\Delta}_{q}u\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C2^{N}\|u\|_{L^{2}}+C\sum\limits_{q>N}2^{-q}\|\dot{\Delta}_{q}\omega\|_{L^{\infty}}.

Therefore,

‖u‖L∞≤C​2N​‖u‖L2+C​2−N​‖ω‖L∞.\|u\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C2^{N}\|u\|_{L^{2}}+C2^{-N}\|\omega\|_{L^{\infty}}.

Taking NN so that 2N​‖u‖L2≈2−N​‖ω‖L∞2^{N}\|u\|_{L^{2}}\approx 2^{-N}\|\omega\|_{L^{\infty}}, we get the desired inequality.

Proving Inequality (15) relies on the similar decomposition into low and high frequencies. The details are left to the reader.
